lesson.menu_title: The American Executive Conversation -- The Question That Comes Back
lesson.menu_desc: Small talk, rapport and the follow-up code: the echo question that borrows his auxiliary, the three-word question that opens the door again, and the pivot that turns a hallway into business -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- The American Executive Conversation

lesson.grammar_point: echo questions and short follow-up questions

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: an interest or experience that two people share and can build a conversation on
a first question or comment that makes two strangers comfortable enough to keep talking
easy to talk to, and never making the other person feel small
to make short contact with someone, so that the relationship stays alive
light conversation about neutral subjects that people use before the real business starts
to give back the same kind of thing you received, such as returning a question
the easy, friendly connection that makes two people want to keep talking to each other
the level of formality you choose for a situation, from very casual to very formal

paras: In an American office the real meeting almost never starts at the top of the hour. It starts with two or three minutes about the weekend, the flight, the coffee, the traffic. To someone who learned English from technical documentation this looks like time that could be saved, and the temptation is to skip it and open the agenda. That is a mistake, because those two minutes are where rapport is built, and rapport decides how the next fifty go. The topics are deliberately light and low-risk: travel, food, sport, the city, the conference itself, the weather. Money, politics, religion, age and health stay out. The point is never the topic. The point is finding common ground fast, so that two strangers stop being strangers before the difficult part begins.

The engine of that conversation is the follow-up question, and this is where a careful speaker usually stops too early. An American says something about himself and then waits. If nothing comes back, the conversation dies, and he reads the silence as a lack of interest, not as politeness and not as a language problem. Two very short moves keep it alive. The first is the echo question: he says "I just moved back from Tokyo", and you say "Oh, did you?" You are not asking for information. You are showing that you heard him and that you want the rest. The second is the short follow-up, three or four words that open the door again: "How so?" "Such as?" "What kind?" "Since when?" And when he asks you something, you answer and then you reciprocate, because in an American conversation the ball is never supposed to stay on one side.

The last piece is register, and it moves while you talk. Small talk is casual: contractions, short sentences, first names from the first minute, even with someone far above you in the company. The moment the business starts, the register goes up a level, and so does the precision: fuller sentences, numbers, no jokes about the thing you are about to propose. Knowing when to make that turn is a skill in itself, and the turn has a sound. "So, you mentioned you were rebuilding the platform." One word, one pause, and everybody in the hallway knows the small talk is over. What Americans remember a week later is rarely how correct your English was. It is whether you were approachable, whether you asked them anything at all, and whether you said you would touch base and then did.

gapfill.text: Two moves keep an American conversation alive. The echo question borrows the auxiliary of his sentence: "I moved back from Tokyo" gives you "Oh, did you?" The short follow-up opens the door again in three words: "How so?" "Such as?" "What kind?" Then you reciprocate, and the question goes back to him.

bank.label: Lines that keep the conversation going
items: Oh, did you? How long were you there?
Have you? What keeps you coming back?
How so?
Such as?
That must have been a big change.
Forty years, most of them at IBM. How about you?
So, you mentioned you were rebuilding the platform.
Let me touch base with you after the summit.

forms.title: Five moves that keep the other person talking
cards: "I just moved back from Tokyo." gives you "Oh, did you?" Take the auxiliary of his sentence, keep the tense, keep it positive. No auxiliary in the sentence? Borrow do, does or did.
"How so?" "Such as?" "What kind?" "Since when?" They cost you almost nothing, they take no floor away from him, and they open the door again.
"Forty years, most of them at IBM. How about you?" The ball is never supposed to stay on one side, and four words are enough to return it.
Find it in the first minute
"You were at the Toronto summit too? So was I." One shared thing is enough to build a whole conversation on, and it is why the light topics work.
"So, you mentioned you were rebuilding the platform." That is how the small talk ends, the register goes up a level and the business starts, without anybody feeling interrupted.

items.situation: At a conference, a stranger tells you he has just come back from three years in Singapore. React so that he keeps talking.
tips: Oh, have you? What took you there?
The echo borrows his auxiliary -- have -- and the short question asks for the story.

items.situation: He says: "We rolled out the new platform last quarter." Show interest without taking the floor away from him.
tips: Did you? How did that go?
Past simple carries no auxiliary, so the echo borrows did.

items.situation: He says: "Honestly, the migration was harder than we expected." Ask for the detail in three words.
tips: Three words are enough. A long question would move the conversation to you.

items.situation: He asks how long you have been working in technology. Answer and keep the conversation balanced.
tips: More than forty years, most of them at IBM. How about you?
Answer first, then reciprocate: the ball goes straight back.

items.situation: The small talk has run for three minutes and you need to start the real conversation. Make the turn.
tips: So, you mentioned you were rebuilding the platform.
One word, one pause, and the register goes up a level.

items: Round 1 -- Guided
Your teacher gives you five statements about herself, one at a time. React to each one with the correct echo question and nothing else. Get the auxiliary right before you add anything.
Round 2 -- Echo and open
Same five statements. This time add one short follow-up after the echo, and let her talk for at least fifteen seconds before you speak again.
Round 3 -- Three real minutes
Hold a three-minute hallway conversation with your teacher as a stranger at a summit. Find common ground in the first minute and ask at least four questions.
Curveball
Halfway through, she mentions that her team is hiring. Make the pivot from small talk to business, and close by offering to touch base.

answerkey.title: Reveal the marked-up model conversation
list: HIM: "First time here? I flew in from Boston last night." -- YOU: "Oh, did you? [ECHO] How was the flight?" [SHORT FOLLOW-UP]
HIM: "Long. I have been doing this trip once a month since January." -- YOU: "Have you? [ECHO, present perfect] That is a lot of miles. What takes you here so often?"
HIM: "We are rebuilding the platform and the vendor is here." -- YOU: "Are you? [ECHO, verb to be] How so -- is it a full rebuild or a migration?" [SHORT FOLLOW-UP]

HIM: "A full rebuild. And you, what brings you to the summit?" -- YOU: "The safety track. I spent most of my career on infrastructure and moved into safety two years ago. How about you?" [ANSWER + RECIPROCATE]
HIM: "Policy first, engineering later. We are hiring on that side, actually." -- YOU: "So, you mentioned the safety track -- what does that team look like today?" [THE PIVOT: the register goes up]
YOU, to close: "This was useful. Let me touch base with you after the summit, once you are back in Boston." [NEXT STEP]
answerkey.note: Read the model once, then run the same shape with your own facts. What matters is the ORDER -- echo, short question, answer and return, pivot, next step -- not these exact words.

listenings.text: I have spent about fifteen years now watching senior people work a room, and I do something at those events that sounds strange when I say it out loud. I count. I stand near two people who are talking, and I count how many questions each of them asks. The number is almost never equal. One of them asks eight questions in ten minutes and the other asks none, and when they walk away, I already know which one will get the follow-up email. It has nothing to do with charm and nothing to do with language. The person who asked is the one who will be remembered, because a week later nobody remembers what the other person said. They remember how they felt while they were saying it, and people feel good when someone is genuinely interested in them. So here is the part that senior people resist the most. You do not have to be interesting. That is a huge relief, and almost nobody believes me the first time. You have to be interested, which is a completely different job and a much easier one. And when you run out of things to say, which happens to everybody, do not change the subject and do not reach for a new topic. Go back to the last thing the other person said and ask about it in three words. How so. Such as. Since when. That is the entire technique. It fits on the back of a business card, and I have watched it change careers.

Note to myself before I forget the details of this afternoon. Final round with the infrastructure candidate, one hour, and I want to be very clear about why I am hesitating, because it is not the obvious thing. The answers were strong. Clear, well structured, real numbers in them, and when I pushed on the failed program he did not get defensive, which is rare. On paper this is a yes. But something was off for the whole hour and it took me until the parking lot to name it. He never asked me anything. Not one question, not about the team, not about the roadmap, not about why the role is open, not even about me. So the hour felt like a test he was passing rather than a conversation between two people who might work together on Monday. And that matters here, because the job is eighty percent talking to people who do not report to him. If he cannot get curious with the person deciding whether to hire him, I do not know what he does in a room with a vendor. So two things. Keep him in the process, I am not saying no. And when you brief the next ones, tell them from me to bring two or three real questions and to ask them early, in the middle of the conversation, not saved up for the last four minutes when everybody is already looking at the clock.

extra_audio.text: First I open with something light about the place or the trip. Then I listen for one thing we have in common. When he tells me something, I echo it with the auxiliary he used. After that I ask one short follow-up question and let him talk. And before I leave, I say I will touch base, and I write his name down.
